      10. The Lebesgue and Riemann integrals#

      The Riemann integral introduced in Note 1 uses upper and lower sums over partitions of an interval. The Lebesgue integral developed in Notes 19–22 instead measures level sets. Both constructions assign an area to a bounded function on , so we now determine when their values agree.

      Semicontinuity gives a useful description of the local behavior of a bounded function. Its lower and upper semicontinuous envelopes record the smallest and largest values that remain visible in arbitrarily small neighborhoods. The two envelopes agree at exactly the points of continuity. We use this description to prove Lebesgue’s criterion: a bounded function is Riemann integrable exactly when its discontinuity set has Lebesgue measure zero. In that case, the function is Lebesgue integrable and the two integrals coincide. We then approximate every continuous function from below by an increasing sequence of Lipschitz functions.

      After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

      • Recognize lower and upper semicontinuous functions from their level sets.

      • Construct the lower and upper semicontinuous envelopes of a bounded function.

      • Identify the discontinuity set as the set where the two envelopes differ.

      • Prove that a bounded function is Riemann integrable if and only if its discontinuity set has Lebesgue measure zero.

      • Prove that the Lebesgue and Riemann integrals agree whenever the bounded function is Riemann integrable.

      • Approximate a continuous function uniformly from below by Lipschitz functions defined through an infimum formula.

      Throughout these notes, are real numbers, carries Lebesgue measure, and all neighborhoods are understood relative to . We write for the Lebesgue integral unless the type of integral is displayed explicitly.

      10.1 One-sided forms of continuity#

      Continuity controls a function from above and below near each point. Some functions satisfy only one of these two controls. For example, the indicator of an open set can jump upward at the boundary of the set, but it cannot jump downward there. Lower semicontinuity describes this behavior.

      Definition 1 (Lower and upper semicontinuity)#

      A function is lower semicontinuous at if, for every , there exists such that It is upper semicontinuous at if, for every , there exists such that The function is lower semicontinuous, abbreviated LSC, or upper semicontinuous, abbreviated USC, when the corresponding condition holds at every point of .

      Thus lower semicontinuity prevents nearby values from falling a fixed amount below ; upper semicontinuity prevents them from rising a fixed amount above . A function is continuous if and only if it is both LSC and USC.

      The definitions can also be read from level sets. A function is LSC if and only if is open in for every . Similarly, is USC if and only if is open in for every . Consequently, every LSC or USC function is Borel measurable.

      These examples also show that semicontinuity does not imply continuity. An indicator may have a jump at every boundary point of its defining set.

      10.3 Agreement of the two integrals#

      The envelope description separates a function into a semicontinuous part and its values at the discontinuities. The Riemann integral exists precisely when the set supporting this gap has Lebesgue measure zero. This is the criterion previewed in Note 1.

      Theorem 8 (Lebesgue’s criterion and agreement of the integrals)#

      2. Its discontinuity set has Lebesgue measure zero.

      Corollary 9 (Agreement for continuous functions)#

      If is continuous, then its Riemann and Lebesgue integrals exist and are equal.

      10.4 Lipschitz approximation from below#
